en: Now begins the Dhātupāṭha of Pāṇini.
1.1 *bhū* in the sense of existence. It is accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) and is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
Now follow those ending in the *tavarga* (dental) group:
1.4 *gādhṛ* in the senses of standing firm, desiring support, and tying;
1.5 *bādhṛ* in the sense of agitating and churning;
1.7 *nāthṛ* is used in the senses of begging, distress, seeking power, and benediction;
1.11 *vadi* in the sense of salutation and praise;
1.12 *bhadi* in the sense of auspiciousness and happiness.
1.13 *mad* [is used] in the senses of praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, and gait; 1.14 *spad* [is used] in the sense of slight movement; 1.15 *klid* [is used] in the sense of lamentation.
1.20 *urda* in the sense of measuring and playing;
1.22 *khurda* 1.23 *gurda*: only in the sense of playing with balls. 1.24 *guda*: only in the sense of playing with balls.
1.26 √hrād, in the sense of an indistinct sound. 1.27 √hlād, also in the sense of pleasure.
1.29 *parḍa* in the sense of a contemptible sound;
1.35 *śrathi* in the sense of loosening; 1.36 *grathi* in the sense of crookedness.
1.37 *kattha* is used in the sense of boasting. Thus, these roots beginning with *edh* are udātta-anudāttet (having an udātta vowel as their indicatory letter).
1.38 *ata* in the sense of continuous movement;
1.47 *luthi* 1.48 *mathi* in the senses of harming and distressing;
1.50 *ṣidhū* [is used] in the sense of a treatise (*śāstra*) and in the sense of auspiciousness (*māṅgalya*).
1.51 *khādṛ* [is used] in the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*).
1.52 *khada* [is used] in the sense of stability (*sthairya*) and in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*).
1.54 *gada* in the sense of distinct speech;
1.56 *ṇad* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
1.57 *ard* in the sense of going and begging;
1.61 *kard* in the sense of a contemptible sound.
1.68 *gaḍi* in the sense of a part of the face;
1.71 *cad* in the sense of delight and radiance;
1.74 *krad* and 1.75 *klad* [are used] in calling out and weeping;
1.77 *śundha* in the sense of purification; these and others ending in an udātta vowel and having an udātta indicatory letter (*udāttet*) [are ātmanepada].
Now follow those ending in the *ka*-group [consonants]: 1.78 *śīkṛ* in the sense of sprinkling;
1.83 *drekṛ* and 1.84 *dhrekṛ* are used in the sense of shouting or exultation.
1.85 *rekṛ* is used in the sense of apprehension.
1.89 śaki, 1.90 ślaki: these two roots mean "to go" (gatyarthāḥ).
1.92 *aki* in the sense of perceiving; 1.93 *vaki* in the sense of crookedness;
1.98 *caka* in the sense of satisfaction and obstruction; 1.99 *kaki*; 1.100 *vaki*.
1.101 śvakṛ (to bark) 1.102 trakṛ (to cry out) 1.103 ḍhaukṛ (to approach)
1.114 Some say [the root] is *ṣvaki*; others say the third [consonant] begins with a dental. *Laghi* is also used in the sense of "ceasing from eating. 1.115 *aghi*.

1.116 *vaghi* and 1.117 *maghi*: [mean] "to move with haste" (*gatyākṣepa*). Others say [they mean] "in motion" (*gati*) and "the commencement of motion" (*gatyārambha*). *Maghi* also means "in deceit" (*kaitava*). 1.118 *rāghṛ*.
1.121 Some also include *dhrāghṛ*. *Drāghṛ* also means extension.
1.122 *ślāghṛ* [is used] in the sense of boasting. Thus, the roots beginning with *śī* are udātta and have anudātta vowels as their indicatory markers (*it*).
1.123 *phakka* in the sense of going low; 1.124 *taka* in the sense of laughing; 1.125 *taki* in the sense of living with difficulty.
1.126 *bukka* in the sense of barking; 1.127 *śuka* in the sense of going;
1.129 okhṛ (to move) 1.130 rākhṛ (to protect) 1.131 lākhṛ (to take)
1.150 īkṣa (to look at) 1.151 īkhi (to go) 1.152 valga (to leap)
1.165 One hundred and sixty-five roots have the meaning of "motion.

1.180 *ghaggh*—some say [it means laughing]. 1.181 *daghi*—in the sense of protecting. 1.182 *laghi*—in the sense of drying up, in common usage also in the sense of shining and transgressing a boundary.
1.183 *maghi* in the sense of adorning; 1.184 *śighi* in the sense of smelling;
1.185 *argha* in the sense of price. These, beginning with *phakka*, are roots with an udātta vowel that have an udātta indicatory letter (*udāttet*).
Now follow those ending in the *c*-group:
1.187 *ṣac* in the sense of sprinkling and serving.
1.189 *śaca* in the sense of distinct speech;
1.194 *kāci* [is used] in the sense of binding and shining.
1.196 *muci* [is used] in the sense of deceit; others say it means "to tell."
1.197 *maci* in the sense of holding, raising, and honoring;
1.198 *paci* in the sense of making manifest;
1.199 *ṣṭuca* in the sense of being gracious.
1.200 *ṛj* [is used] in the senses of going straight, standing, acquiring, and earning.
1.202 *bhṛjī* [is used] in the sense of roasting.
1.207 *īja* in the senses of motion and censuring.
1.209 *vīja* means "to go. Thus end the *varca*-class roots, which are accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) and followed by an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*).
1.211 *kuc* in the sense of a high-pitched sound;
1.213 *kruñc* in the sense of crookedness and diminution;
1.215 *añc* in the sense of motion and worship.
1.219 tvañcu (to contract) 1.220 mruñcu (to contract) 1.221 mluñcu (to contract)
1.222 *mrucu*, 1.223 *mlucu*: these have the sense of motion.
1.225 *glucu*, 1.226 *kujū*, 1.227 *khujū*— these [roots] mean the act of stealing.
1.228 *gluñca* 1.229 *ṣasja*, *ṣasja* in the sense of "going"; *ṣasji* is also used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). 1.230 *guja*.
1.231 *guji* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
1.233 *mlecha* in the sense of an indistinct sound.
1.235 *lāchi* (in the sense of a characteristic mark);
1.238 *hrī-cha* in the sense of modesty; 1.239 *hur-chā* in the sense of crookedness.
1.240 *murchā* is used in the sense of fainting and rising up.
1.241 *sphurchā* is used in the sense of expansion. 1.242 *yucha* is used in the sense of negligence.
1.243 *uchi* means to glean. 1.244 *uchī* means to dwell. 1.245 *dhraja* [is used in the sense of] moving.
1.254 *kūja* [in the sense of making a sound].
1.255 *kuji* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
1.256 *arja* and 1.257 *ṣarja* in the sense of acquisition.
1.261 *kharja* in the sense of honoring; 1.262 *aja* in the senses of motion and casting away;
1.264 *khaja* means to churn; 1.265 *kaja* means to intoxicate, according to some;
1.268 *sphūrjā* (with the augment *ṭu*) in the sense of the roar of a thunderbolt;
1.270 *kṣīj* in the sense of an indistinct sound; 1.271 *laj*;
1.273 *lāja* and 1.274 *lāji* in the sense of threatening;
1.276 *jaji* in the sense of fighting; 1.277 *tuja* in the sense of harming; 1.278 *tuji* in the sense of protecting.
1.279 gaja (to sound) 1.280 gaji (to roar) 1.281 gṛja (to sound)
1.284 *muji* have the meaning of sound (*śabda*). *Gaja* also means intoxication (*madana*).
1.285 *vaja* and 1.286 *vraja* mean "to go. These, beginning with *śuc*, excluding *kṣi*, are accented on the first syllable and have an udātta indicatory vowel (*udāttet*).
Now follow those ending in the *ṭa*-class consonants:
1.287 *aṭṭa* in the sense of transgression and injury; [that is,] in the sense of transgressing and harming.
1.291 *loṣṭa* in the sense of a clod or mass.
1.292 *ghaṭṭa* means to move. 1.293 *sphuṭa* means to blossom or expand.
1.295 *vaṭhi* in the sense of solitary wandering; 1.296 *maṭhi*;
1.301 *hiḍi* in the sense of movement and disregard;
1.302 *huḍi* in the sense of a collection; 1.303 *kuḍi* in the sense of enclosing.
1.304 *vaḍi* in the sense of dividing; 1.305 *maḍi* also [in that sense];
1.307 *piḍi* in the sense of compressing; 1.308 *muḍi* in the sense of cleaning;
1.310 *huḍi* in the sense of choosing; some say in the sense of taking away. 1.311 *sphuḍi* in the sense of blossoming. 1.312 *caḍi* in the sense of anger.
1.313 *śaḍi* in the sense of pain and accumulation;
1.314 *taḍi* in the sense of striking; 1.315 *paḍi* in the sense of going.
1.316 *kaḍi* means to intoxicate; 1.317 *khaḍi* means to churn; 1.318 *heḍṛ*.
1.319 *hoḍṛ* in the sense of disregard; 1.320 *bāḍṛ* in the sense of flooding;
1.322 *drāḍṛ* and 1.323 *dhrāḍṛ* are used in the sense of breaking.
1.324 *śāḍṛ* is used in the sense of praising. These roots beginning with *aṭṭ* are udātta and have anudātta indicatory letters (*anudāttet*).
1.325 śauṭṛ, to be proud; 1.326 yauṭṛ, to bind; 1.327 mreṭṛ.
1.330 *kaṭe* in the senses of raining and covering.
1.331 Some say *caṭ* [means "to move"]. 1.332 *aṭ*. 1.333 *paṭ*, in the sense of "going."
1.334 *raṭ* in the sense of reviling; 1.335 *laṭ* in the sense of childhood;
1.336 *śaṭ* in the senses of sickness, breaking apart, motion, and exhaustion.
1.347 *ṇaṭa* and *naṭa* in the sense of dancing;
1.348 *piṭa* in the sense of sound and collection.
1.349 *haṭa* in the sense of shining; 1.350 *ṣaṭa* in the sense of a limb;
1.352 Some say that *luḍ* ends in *ḍ*; others say that this [root] ends in *ḍ*. 1.353 *ciṭ* means "to command another. 1.354 *viṭ* means "sound."
1.364 *muḍa* 1.365 *puḍa* in the sense of crushing or grinding;
1.367 Some say that *puṭ* means "to fold. 1.368 *cuḍi* means "to become small. 1.369 *muḍi* means "to break into pieces."
1.371 *ruṭi* and 1.372 *luṭi* [are used] in the sense of stealing.
1.376 Others say [the root] is *luḍi*. 1.377 *vaṭi* means "to divide. 1.378 Some say [the root] is *baṭi*.
1.379 *sphuṭir* in the sense of breaking apart;
1.381 *paṭha* in the sense of distinct speech.
1.384 *maṭha* in the senses of intoxication and dwelling.
1.385 *kaṭha* means to live with difficulty. 1.386 *raṭha* means to revile.
1.388 *Haṭha* means forceful exertion (*pluti*) or deceit (*śaṭhatva*); others say it means compulsion (*balātkāra*). 1.389 *Ruṭha*; 1.390 *Luṭha*.
1.393 *piṭha* in the senses of harming and distressing.
1.394 *śaṭh* is used in the sense of deceit (*kaitava*). 1.395 *śuṭh* is used in the sense of obstruction to movement (*gatipratighāta*) and striking (*pratighāta*).
1.397 *kuṭhi* also [in the sense of being crooked]. 1.398 *luṭhi* in the sense of laziness and striking. 1.399 *śuṭhi* in the sense of drying up.
1.402 *cuḍḍa*, *cudḍa* in the sense of producing a state of being.

1.403 *aḍḍ* and *adḍ* are used in the sense of "assault. 1.404 *kaḍḍ* and *kadḍ* are used in the sense of "roughness. *cuḍḍ* and the two following [roots] have *d* as their penultimate letter (*dopadha*). 1.405 *krīḍṛ* is used in the sense of "sporting."
1.416 Some say that *lal* means to desire. 1.417 *kaḍ* means to intoxicate.
1.419 *gaḍi* [means] "in one part of the face. Thus, *śauṭra* and the others are roots with an acute accent on the first syllable (*udātta*) and an indicatory letter *ṇ* (*udāttet*).
Now follow those ending in the *pavarga* [labial] class:
1.422 *ṣṭipṛ*, 1.423 *ṣṭepṛ*: these two have the meaning "to flow. The first is anudātta (unaccented). *tepṛ* also means "to tremble. 1.424 *glepṛ*: to be dejected.
1.437 *labi* 1.438 *abi* in the sense of sound; 1.439 *labi* also in the sense of falling down.
1.440 *kabṛ* in the sense of color; 1.441 *klībṛ* in the sense of lack of courage; 1.442 *kṣībṛ* in the sense of intoxication.
1.446 cībhṛ (to eat) | 1.447 rebhṛ (in the sense of sound) | 1.448 abhi- [root *rabh*] (to begin, to undertake).
1.449 Some read *rabhi* in certain places; 1.450 and *labhi*;
1.452 *skabh* in the sense of obstructing; 1.453 *jabhī*; 1.454 *jṛbhi* in the sense of bending the limbs.
1.455 *śalbha* in the sense of boasting; 1.456 *valbha* in the sense of eating;
1.459 some say *srambhu*, beginning with a dental [sibilant];
1.460 *ṣṭubhu* in the sense of supporting. These roots beginning with *ti* are udātta and have anudātta vowels, excluding *tip*.
1.461 *gup* in the sense of protecting; 1.462 *dhūp* in the sense of heating;
1.464 *jalpa* means "in distinct speech" and *japa* means "in mental [recitation]. 1.465 *capa* means "in consoling.
1.467 *rapa* and 1.468 *lapa* [are used] in the sense of distinct speech;
1.469 *cupa* [is used] in the sense of slow movement.
1.476 *trupha* and 1.477 *trumpha* have the meaning of "to injure.
1.485 *marba* (one million billion) 1.486 *karba* (ten million billion) 1.487 *kharba* (one hundred million billion)
1.491 *carba* in the sense of moving; and in the sense of eating. 1.492 *kubi* in the sense of covering or concealing. 1.493 *lubi*...
1.494 *tubi* in the sense of crushing; 1.495 *cubi* in the sense of joining the mouth; 1.496 *ṣṛbhu*.

1.500 *śubha* and 1.501 *śumbha* [are used] in the sense of speaking; some say in the sense of shining, others in the sense of harming. Thus end the roots beginning with *gup*, which are udātta and have an udātta indicatory letter (*udāttet*).
Now follow those ending in nasals:
1.507 *paṇ* in the sense of bargaining and praising;

1.511 *kamū* in the sense of desiring. These, beginning with *ghiṇ*, are roots that have an udātta accent on the root vowel and are marked as having an anudātta accent on the radical vowel (*anudāttet*).
1.512 aṇa (to breathe) 1.513 raṇa (to sound) 1.514 vaṇa (to speak)
1.518 kvaṇa (to sound); 1.519 vraṇa, braṇa (to wound); 1.520 bhraṇa (to kill).
1.524 *śoṇṛ* in the sense of moving with a particular color; 1.525 *śroṇṛ* in the sense of collecting together; 1.526 *śloṇṛ* also [in this sense].
1.527 *paiṇṛ* [is used] in the senses of moving, impelling, and joining.
1.531 *kanī* in the senses of shining, beauty, and motion.
1.536 *am* in the senses of going and so forth—namely, going, sound, and sharing;
1.538 *hamm* (to strike); 1.539 *mīmṛ* (in the sense of going; and in the sense of sound); 1.540 *camu*.
1.544 Some say [the root] is *jimu*. 1.545 *kramu* means "to step. These roots beginning with *aṇ* are udātta and have an udātta indicatory vowel (*udāttet*).
Now follow those ending in ya, ra, la, and va:
1.551 *ṇaya* means "to go"; it also means "to protect. 1.553 *daya* means "giving," "going," "protecting," "harming," and "taking."
1.554 *raya* in the sense of going; 1.555 *laya* also [in that sense];
1.556 *ūyī* in the sense of weaving or extending a thread.
1.557 *pūyī* in the sense of decaying and having a foul odor; 1.558 *knūyī* in the sense of sounding and wetting;
1.563 *śala* in the senses of moving and covering;
1.564 *vala*; 1.565 *valla* in the senses of covering and moving.
1.569 *bhalla* in the sense of reviling, harming, and giving;
1.570 *kala* in the sense of sound and counting;
1.571 *kalla* in the sense of indistinct sound; some say it means "not sound."
1.575 gevṛ (to move) 1.576 glevṛ (to move) 1.577 pevṛ (to move)
1.578 mṛvṛ, 1.579 mlavṛ, 1.580 śevṛ: these [roots] mean service. 1.580 śevṛ.
1.584 *revṛ* (to leap, to move) — thus end the roots beginning with *i*, which are udātta and have anudātta indicatory letters (*anudāttet*).
1.585 *mavya* in the sense of binding; 1.586 *sūrkṣya* and *sūrkṣya*; 1.587 *īrkṣya*.
1.588 *īrṣya* [is used] in the sense of envy; 1.589 *haya* in the sense of going;
1.592 *harya* in the senses of motion and desire;
1.593 *ala* in the senses of ornamenting, sufficiency, and prohibition. According to some, this [root *ala*] is *svarita*-accented.
1.594 *ñiphala* in the sense of falling apart; 1.595 *mīla*; 1.596 *śmīla*.
1.600 *ṇīla* in the sense of color; 1.601 *śīla* in the sense of concentration;
1.603 *kūla* in the sense of covering; 1.604 *śūla* in the sense of pain and also in the sense of a collection;
1.606 *pūla* in the sense of gathering together;
1.609 *culla* in the sense of making something small; 1.610 *phulla* in the sense of blooming; 1.611 *cilla* in the sense of looseness and also in the sense of making something small.
1.612 *tila* means "to go. 1.613 Some say [the root] is *tilla*.
1.615 celṛ (to move) 1.616 kelṛ (to move) 1.617 khelṛ (to move)
1.624 Some say that *ṣelṛ* [is used] in this sense.
1.625 *skhala* in the sense of moving about; 1.626 *khala* in the sense of accumulation and so forth.
1.627 *gala* in the senses of swallowing, eating, and flowing;
1.629 *dala* in the sense of splitting apart.
1.633 *khorṛ* in the sense of obstructing movement;
1.634 *dhorṛ* in the sense of skillfulness in movement;
1.635 *tsara* in the sense of moving by means of deception.
1.639 *mabhra* 1.640 *cara*. These roots have the sense of "going. *Carati* also has the sense of "eating";
*cara* [is used] in the sense of eating, and *carati* also [is used] in the sense of eating.
1.641 *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of spitting out; 1.642 *ji* in the sense of victory;
1.643 *jīva* in the sense of sustaining life.
1.644 pīva (to swell) 1.645 mīva (to swell) 1.646 tīva (to swell)
1.647 ṇīv- in the sense of stoutness;
1.648 kṣiv- and 1.649 kṣev- in the sense of casting out.
1.653 *durvī* and 1.654 *dhurvī* have the sense of harming;
1.655 *gurvī* has the sense of lifting up.
1.659 *marva* in the sense of filling; 1.660 *carva* in the sense of eating;
1.673 *ṇivi* [mean] "in the act of sprinkling. Some say they mean "in the act of sprinkling."
1.674 Some say that *ṣivi* means "to serve"; in the *Taraṅgiṇī*, it is said to mean "to serve.
1.677 *dhivi* and 1.678 *jivi* have the meaning of "pleasing" or "delighting. 1.679 *rivi*.

1.684 *ava* in the senses of protection, motion, beauty, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entering, hearing, ownership, requesting, action, desire, splendor, attainment, embracing, injury, giving, sharing, and increase.
Thus, the roots beginning with *mavy*, with the exception of *jaya*, are acute-accented and have an acute-accented vowel as their indicatory letter (*udātta-it*).
1.685 *dhāv* [is used] in the senses of motion and purification; it is both udātta and svarita.
Now follow those ending in the sibilant *ūṣman*:
1.686 *dhukṣa* and 1.687 *dhikṣa*, in the senses of inflaming, afflicting, and living.
1.688 *vṛkṣ* in the sense of covering; 1.689 *śikṣ* in the sense of acquiring knowledge;
1.690 *bhikṣ* in the sense of begging, whether there be no gain or gain.
1.691 *Kleśa* [is used] in the sense of indistinct speech; others say it means "affliction," according to Durga.
1.692 *Dakṣa* [is used] in the sense of growth and speed.
1.693 *Dīkṣa* [is used] in the sense of shaving the head, sacrifice, initiation (*upanayana*), religious observances (*niyama*), and the instruction of vows (*vrata*).
1.694 *īkṣ* in the sense of seeing; 1.695 *īṣ* in the senses of motion, injury, and seeing;
1.696 *bhāṣ* in the sense of distinct speech.
1.703 jeṣṛ (to conquer) 1.704 ṇeṣṛ (to lead) 1.705 eṣṛ (to go)
1.709 *hreṣṛ* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
1.710 *kāsṛ* in the sense of contemptuous sound;
1.712 ṇāsṛ, 1.713 rāsṛ in the sense of sound;
1.714 ṇasa in the sense of crookedness.
1.715 *bhyas* [is used] in the sense of fear;
1.716 *āṅ-śas* [is used] in the sense of desire; 1.717 *grasu*.
1.719 *īh* in the sense of effort or exertion;
1.721 *mahi* in the sense of increasing; 1.722 *ahi* in the sense of moving;
1.725 *barha* and 1.726 *balha* in the sense of preeminence.
1.727 *varha* and 1.728 *valha* are used in the senses of reviling, injuring, and covering;
1.729 *pliha* is used in the sense of going.
1.730 *vehṛ* and *behṛ*; 1.731 *jehṛ*; 1.732 *bāhṛ* and *vāhṛ* in the sense of exertion (*prayatna*); *jehṛ* also in the sense of going (*gati*).
1.733 *drāhṛ* [is used] in the sense of the cessation of sleep; some say in the sense of depositing.
1.738 *glaha* also [in the sense of seizing], with the sense of taking away as its specific application.
1.739 *ghuṣi* in the sense of making beautiful;
1.740 some say *ghaṣa*. Thus end the roots beginning with *dhukṣ*, which are udātta and have anudātta indicatory letters (*anudāttet*).
1.741 *ghuṣir* in the sense of "not making sound"; others read it as "making sound.
1.744 *tvakṣū* in the sense of making thin; 1.745 *ukṣa* in the sense of sprinkling;
1.747 ṇikṣa, in the sense of kissing; 1.748 trakṣa;
1.753 *vakṣa* in the sense of anger; some say in the sense of a mass.
1.754 *mṛkṣa* in the sense of a mass;
1.757 Some say that *pakṣa* means "to embrace" or "to take as a side.
1.765 *dhvākṣi* in the sense of making a terrible sound; 1.766 some say *dhmākṣi*;
1.775 *yūṣ* in the sense of "injuring"; 1.776 and *jūṣ* as well.
1.783 śiṣa (to sharpen) 1.784 jaṣa (to eat) 1.785 jhaṣa (to eat)
1.789 *ruṣ* and 1.790 *riṣ* have the meaning "to injure. 1.791 *bhaṣ* means "to scold."
1.795 miṣu, 1.796 ṇiṣu, in the sense of sprinkling;
1.797 puṣa, in the sense of nourishing.
1.801 pluṣu (to burn) 1.802 pṛṣu (to sprinkle) 1.803 vṛṣu (to rain, to pour down)
1.804 *mṛṣu* means to sprinkle; and also to endure. The other two [roots] mean both to injure and to afflict.
1.806 *hṛṣu* means to be false or deceitful.
1.810 *ras* in the sense of sounding; 1.811 *lasa* in the senses of clinging and playing;
1.815 *jhartsa*, *jharjha*, *jharja*—[these roots] are used in the senses of reviling, injuring, and threatening.
1.816 pisṛ (to go) 1.817 pesṛ (to go) 1.818 visṛ (to go)
1.822 *has* in the sense of laughing; 1.823 *ṇiś* in the sense of concentration;
1.829 *śaṃsu* in the sense of praise. Durga states that some [authorities] hold it also means "to fall into misfortune. 1.830 *caha* in the sense of deceit.
1.831 *maha* in the sense of worship; 1.832 *raha* in the sense of abandonment;
1.837 *bṛhi* and *vṛhi* mean "to grow. *Bṛhi* and *vṛhi* also mean "to sound. Some say that *bṛhi* and *vṛhi* are two distinct roots. 1.838 *tuhi*.

1.839 *duhir* and 1.840 *uhir* are used in the sense of "afflicting"; 1.841 *arha* is used in the sense of "worship. Thus, the roots beginning with *ghuṣi* are udātta and have an udātta indicatory letter (*udāttet*).
1.845 *ñiṣvidā* means "moistening" and "releasing," or "the trickling from the limbs";
1.846 Some say [the root] *ñikṣvidā* [is used in the sense of "to sound"]. 1.847 *Ruc* in the sense of shining and taking pleasure. 1.848 *Ghuṭa* in the sense of turning around.
1.852 *uṭh* in the sense of striking and repelling;
1.854 *kṣubh* in the sense of moving or shaking.
1.855 *ṇabha* and 1.856 *tubha* in the sense of "injury"; the first also in the sense of "non-existence. 1.857 *sraṃsu*, *śraṃsu*, *śraṃśu*.

1.858 *dhvaṃsu* and 1.859 *bhraṃsu* [are used] in the sense of falling down (*avasraṃsana*). *Dhvaṃsu* is also used in the sense of going (*gati*). Some maintain that 1.860 *bhraṃśu* is also [included]; others hold that the third [root] alone ends in a palatal (*tālavya*) letter.
1.864 *śṛdhu* in the sense of contemptuous sound;

1.866 *kṛpū* in the sense of capability. [The section] ends. Thus end the roots beginning with *dyut*, which are accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) and have an unaccented vowel as their penultimate (*anudāttet*).
Now, *ghaṭ* and others are measured [as follows]:
1.868 *vyath* in the sense of fear and trembling.
1.869 *prath* in the sense of making known;
1.872 *skhada* in the sense of moving; 1.873 *kṣaji* in the senses of going and giving;
1.874 *dakṣa* in the senses of going and harming, or going and teaching.
*Vṛddhi* is used in the sense of growth and speed (1.875). *Kṛpa* is used in the sense of compassion and going (1.876). Some say *krapa* [is also used].
1.880 *kladim* in the sense of dejection; some say in the sense of deficiency. 1.881 *kadām*. 1.882 *kradām*.
1.884 *ñitvar* in the sense of agitation; the roots beginning with *ghaṭ* are *mit*. Thus, the roots beginning with *ghaṭ* are *udātta* and have an *anudātta* indicatory vowel (*it*).
1.888 *vaṭ* and 1.889 *bhaṭ* in the sense of addressing or reproaching.
1.890 *ṇaṭ* in the sense of dancing; some say in the sense of bowing; others say in the sense of going. 1.891 *ṣṭak* in the sense of striking back or repelling. 1.892 *cak* in the sense of satiety.
1.893 *kakhem* means to laugh; 1.894 *ragem* means apprehension; 1.895 *lagem* means attachment.
1.900 *kageṃ* is not mentioned [as a root], because its meaning is general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). Others say it is because it has multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*).
1.902 *agam* in the sense of moving crookedly;
1.915 *van* also is not spoken of and is not perceived.
1.917 *hvala* and 1.918 *hmla* mean moving or shaking. 1.919 *smṛ* means reflection or meditation.
1.920 *dṛīm* in the sense of fear; 1.921 *nṛīm* in the sense of leading; 1.922 *śrām* in the sense of cooking.
1.923 || [The suffix] *jñā* is used in the senses of killing (*māraṇa*), satisfying (*toṣaṇa*), and sharpening (*niśāmana*). There is an alternative reading: *māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāneṣu*.
1.924 || The root *cal* [is used] in the sense of shaking.
1.925 || *chadiḥ* [is used] in the sense of strengthening (*ūrjana*).
1.926 || *laḍi* [is used] in the sense of licking the tongue.
1.927 || *madī* [is used] in the sense of exhilaration and stupefaction.
1.932 || To roar || 1.933 || Sound || 1.934 || To be ashamed ||
1.935 || And "kṣapaya" [is used] in the sense of "bhoja" (eating/consuming), according to Bhoja.

1.937 janī (to be born) 1.938 jṛīṣ (to grow old) 1.939 knasu (to destroy)
1.940 || And [the suffixes] *man* and *tṛ* are added after the root *rañj*.
1.944 || Or [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *nama*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).
1.953 || *Yama* [is used] in the sense of not serving food.
1.954 || [The suffix *ṇamul* is also applied after the root *khad* when preceded by the prefixes *ava* and *pari*.]
1.955 *phaṇam* (to go; to move and to shine). [End of] the *vṛt* section.

Thus, the *ghaṭa*-group ending with *phaṇ* are marked as *mit*. Thus, the *jvara*-group are acutely accented (*udātta*) roots with an acute accent on the radical vowel (*udāttet*), conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
1.956 *rājṛ* in the sense of shining; it is both udātta and svarita.
1.957 ṭubhrājṛ, 1.958 ṭubhrāśṛ, 1.959 ṭubhlāśṛ: [these roots] mean "to shine. These are the udātta-ending roots that have anudātta indicatory vowels (anudāttet).
1.962 *dhvana* (to sound); the roots beginning with *phaṇ* have been completed.
1.963 *ṣama* 1.964 *ṣṭama* [are used] in the sense of non-deficiency (*avaikalya*) and deficiency (*vaikalya*). [The root] *vṛt*.
1.965 *jval* in the sense of blazing; 1.966 *cal* in the sense of trembling;
1.968 ṭala, 1.969 ṭvala, in the sense of being impaired;
1.970 ṣṭhala, in the sense of standing firm.
1.972 *ṇala* in the sense of smell; some say in the sense of binding;
1.974 *bala* means "to breathe" and "the storage of grain" (or "the act of storing grain").
1.980 *hul* in the senses of harming (*hiṃsā*) and restraining (*saṃvaraṇa*).
1.981 *kvath* in the sense of boiling (*niṣpāka*). 1.982 *path* in the sense of going (*gati*).

1.986 *kṣara* in the sense of moving; 1.987 *kṣura* in the sense of collecting. These, beginning with *syam*, are roots that have an udātta accent on the root syllable and take the udātta accent on the affix.
1.988 *ṣaha* in the sense of enduring; it is accented on the first syllable and is anudātta (unaccented).
1.989 *ramu* in the sense of playing. Mādhava says it is *rama*. It is unaccented and has an unaccented *it*-sign.
1.990 *ṣadḷ* (ṣad) in the senses of falling apart, going, and dejection;

1.991 *śadḷ* (śad) in the sense of perishing; 1.992 *kruśa* in the senses of calling out and weeping. These three roots beginning with *ṣad* are unaccented (*anudātta*) and have an accented radical vowel (*udāttet*).
1.993 *kuca* in the sense of pressing together, crookedness, obstruction, and scratching; 1.994 *budha* in the sense of understanding;
1.995 *ruha* in the sense of the birth of a seed and manifestation.
1.996 *kasa* in the sense of "motion. Thus, the roots beginning with *kuca* are udātta and have an udātta indicatory vowel (*it*), whereas *ruhi* has an anudātta indicatory vowel. [The section] ends.
1.997 *hikka* in the sense of an indistinct sound;
1.998 *añcu* in the sense of going and begging;
1.1012 ṇidṛ 1.1013 ṇedṛ [are used] in the senses of contempt and proximity; 1.1014 śṛdhu.
1.1016 *budhi* means to awaken or perceive. 1.1017 *ubundi* means to settle or calm.
1.1018 *veṇṛ* is used in the senses of movement, knowledge, thought, observation, and the playing or grasping of musical instruments.
1.1020 *khanu* is used in the sense of digging or splitting open.
1.1021 *cīvṛ* in the senses of taking up and covering;
1.1023 *cāyṛ* in the senses of honoring and observing.
1.1026 *bheṣṛ* in the sense of fear; some say it means "going."
1.1032 *spaś*—in the sense of both afflicting and touching.
1.1033 *laṣa* in the sense of longing for; 1.1034 *caṣa* in the sense of eating;
1.1036 *jhaṣ* in the senses of seizing and concealing;
1.1037 *bhrakṣ* and 1.1038 *bhlakṣ* in the sense of eating.
1.1039 *bhakṣ* means "to eat," according to Maitreya; 1.1040 *plakṣ* also [means to eat];
1.1042 *māhṛ* in the sense of measuring; 1.1043 *guhū* in the sense of concealing. Thus end the roots beginning with *hikk*, which are udātta and have a svarita indicatory letter (*svaritet*).
1.1044 *śriñ* in the sense of "service. It is udātta and is used in both voices (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
1.1046 *hṛñ* in the sense of taking away;

1.1048 *kṛñ* in the sense of making; 1.1049 *ṇīñ* in the sense of leading. Thus end the roots beginning with *bhṛñ*, which are anudātta and are conjugated in both voices (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
1.1051 *glai*; 1.1052 *mlai* in the sense of the loss of joy.
1.1053 *dyai* in the sense of disparaging; 1.1054 *drai* in the sense of sleeping;
1.1059 *ṣṭyai* in the sense of sound and collection;
1.1065 *gai* in the sense of sound; 1.1066 *śai*; 1.1067 *śrai* in the sense of cooking.
1.1068 In some recensions, the reading is *srai*.
1.1070 *ovai* [are used] in the sense of drying up.
1.1071 *ṣṭai* and 1.1072 *ṣṇai* mean "to entwine. Some say they also mean "to beautify. 1.1073 *daip* means "to purify."
1.1075 *ghrā* in the sense of perceiving odors or smelling;
1.1076 *dhmā* in the sense of sound and contact with fire.
1.1077 ṣṭhā, in the sense of stopping or ceasing from motion;
1.1078 mnā, in the sense of repeated practice;
1.1079 dāṇ, in the sense of giving.
1.1081 *svṛ* in the sense of sound and affliction;
1.1083 *dvṛ* in the sense of concealing and choosing;
1.1086 √ṛ [in the senses of] motion and reaching;
1.1091 *ṣu* in the sense of procreation and sovereignty.
1.1092 śru, in the sense of hearing;
1.1093 dhru, in the sense of steadiness;
1.1098 *ju* is a root belonging to the *sūtra*-tradition, meaning "to go. Thus, the roots beginning with *dhaya* are anudātta and are conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
1.1099 *ṣmiṅ* in the sense of slight laughter;
1.1100 *guṅ* in the sense of indistinct sound;
1.1114 *ruṅ* in the senses of going and anger;
1.1120 *traiṅ* in the sense of protecting. Thus, beginning with *ṣmiṅ*, these [roots] are anudātta and take the ātmanepada endings.
1.1123 *ḍīṅ* in the sense of moving through the air. These three roots, beginning with *pūṅ*, are accented acute (*udātta*) and are conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
1.1124 *tṛ* [is used] in the senses of floating and crossing over. It is udātta and belongs to the *parasmaipada*.
1.1127 *māna* in the sense of honoring; 1.1128 *badha* in the sense of binding. These four roots beginning with *gup* are udātta and have anudātta indicatory letters (*it*).
1.1132 *hada hada* is used for the act of voiding excrement. Thus, the four roots beginning with *rabh*, which have anudātta vowels, are classified as anudāttet.
1.1133 The root *ñikṣvidā* is used in the sense of an indistinct sound; it is accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) because it is marked with the *udātta* accent.
1.1134 *skandi* in the senses of going and drying;
1.1135 *yabha* in the sense of sexual intercourse and perverse sexual intercourse;
1.1136 *ṇam* in the senses of bowing and sound.
1.1145 *kṛṣa* in the sense of scratching or plowing.
1.1146 *daḥ* in the sense of reducing to ashes;
1.1147 *miḥ* in the sense of sprinkling. Thus, *skanda* and the others are anudātta (unaccented) roots with an udātta (accented) vowel as their penultimate.
1.1148 *kit* [is used] in the senses of dwelling and removing disease; it has an udātta accent and is marked with the udātta sign.
1.1149 *dāna* in the sense of breaking or splitting;
1.1150 *śāna* in the sense of sharpening or making bright. These two roots are udātta and svarita.
1.1151 ḍupacaṣ (ḍupac) in the sense of cooking;
1.1152 ṣaca (ṣac) in the sense of gathering together; 1.1153 bhaja (bhaj) in the sense of serving.
Now, the roots beginning with *yaj*: 1.1157 *yaja* [is used] in the senses of worshipping a deity, forming a connection, and giving;
1.1158 *ḍuvapa* and *ṭuvapa* [are used] in the sense of sowing seeds, and also in the sense of cutting.
1.1159 *vaḥ* in the sense of "attaining. Thus end the roots beginning with *pac*, which are anudātta (unaccented) and have a svarita initial vowel; however, *ṣaci* is udātta (accented).
1.1160 *vasa* in the sense of dwelling; it is udātta and anudātta.
1.1163 *hveñ* in the sense of rivalry and sound. These three roots beginning with *veñ* are anudātta (unaccented) and are used in both voices (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
1.1164 *vad* is used in the sense of distinct speech.
1.1165 *aśvi* is used in the senses of motion and increase.
[The section on] *vṛt* is finished. The class beginning with *yaj* is completed. Both this *vadati* and *aśvi* are udātta roots and are parasmaipada. So too are *culumpati* and others.
2.2 *han* in the senses of killing and going. These two are unaccented (*anudātta*) and have an accented initial vowel (*udāttet*).
2.3 *dviṣ* in the sense of being displeased; 2.4 *duh* in the sense of filling; 2.5 *diha* in the sense of accumulation.
2.6 *liha* in the sense of tasting. Thus, *dviṣ* and the others are anudātta [roots] with a svarita [accent on the root vowel].
2.7 *cakṣiṅ* [is used] in the sense of distinct speech; it is also used in the sense of seeing. It is anudātta and has an anudātta *it*.
2.8 *īr* in the senses of motion and trembling;
2.11 *āsa* in the sense of sitting; 2.12 *āṅ-śāsa* in the sense of desiring;
2.14 The root *kas* is used in the senses of going and teaching.
2.15 Some say it is *kas*. 2.16 Others say it is also *kaś*.
2.20 *Piji* means "color. Some say it means "mixing"; others say it means "both"; others say it means "a part"; and still others say it means "an indistinct sound. 2.21 Some say [the root] is *pṛji*.
2.24 *pṛcī* in the sense of mixing or contact. Thus end the roots beginning with *i*, which are udātta and have anudātta indicatory letters (*anudāttet*).
2.25 *ṣūṅ* in the sense of the delivery of the fetus of living beings;
2.26 *śīṅ* in the sense of sleeping. These two are udātta [roots] conjugated in the ātmanepada.
2.27 *yu* is used in the sense of mixing and sprinkling.
2.28 *ru* is used in the sense of sound.
2.29 *tu* is used in the senses of motion, increase, and injury; it is a verbal root belonging to the *sūtra* (the grammatical tradition).
2.33 *ṣṇu* in the sense of flowing forth. Thus, beginning with *yū*, these [roots] are accented acute and are conjugated in the Parasmaipada.
2.34 The root *ūrṇu* means "to cover. It is udātta and is conjugated in both voices (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
2.36 *ṣu* in the sense of procreation and sovereignty;
2.38 *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of praising. Thus, the roots beginning with *dyu* are anudātta and parasmaipada; *stu* (stauti), however, is ubhayapada.
2.39 *brūñ*, *brūñ*: in the sense of distinct speech. It is accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) and is spoken in both ways (as a root and as a verb).
2.41 *iṅ* in the sense of "studying"; it is always preceded by the prefix *adhi*. 2.42 *ik* in the sense of "remembering"; this one also is preceded by *adhi*.
2.43 *vī* is used in the senses of motion, procreation, beauty, throwing, and eating.
2.44 *yā* is used in the sense of reaching.
2.45 *vā* is used in the senses of motion and scenting.
2.47 *ṣṇā* in the sense of cleansing; 2.48 *śrā* in the sense of cooking.
2.49 *drā* in the sense of loathing and motion; 2.50 *psā* in the sense of eating;
2.53 *lā* in the sense of taking and giving—Candra says both mean "giving";
2.55 *khyā* in the sense of narrating; 2.56 *prā* in the sense of filling; 2.57 *mā* in the sense of measuring.
2.58 *vaca* is used in the sense of speaking. The roots beginning with *iṇ* are *anudātta* (unaccented) and are *parasmaipada* (active voice); however, *iṅ* is *ātmanepada* (middle voice).
2.60 *as* in the sense of existence; 2.61 *mṛjū* and *mṛjūṣ* in the sense of purification.
2.62 *rudir* (to shed tears). Thus, the *vid*-class roots ending in an acute accent (*udātta*) are [those whose] indicatory letter (*it*) is acute.
2.63 The root *ñiṣvap* (to sleep) is unaccented (*anudātta*), because it is taught with an acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable.
2.64 *śvas* [is used] in the sense of breathing.
2.65 *ana* [is also used in that sense]. Now, the roots beginning with *jakṣ* [are to be considered as having reduplicated present stems].
2.66 *jakṣ* [is used] in the senses of eating and laughing. [The rule] *vṛt* [applies]. Thus end the roots beginning with *rud*. 2.67 *jāgṛ* [is used] in the sense of the cessation of sleep.
2.68 *daridrā* [is used] in the sense of being in a state of poverty or misfortune.

2.69 *cakāsṛ* in the sense of shining; 2.70 *śāsu* in the sense of instructing. These, beginning with *śvas*, are roots that have an udātta accent on the root syllable and take an udātta vowel as their *it*.
2.71 *dīdhīṅ* in the sense of shining and playing;
2.72 *vevīṅ* with a meaning equal to *veti*. These two are udātta and ātmanepadī. [The section] ends here. Thus end the *jakṣityādayaḥ*.

2.73 *ṣasa* (to sleep), 2.74 *ṣasti* (to sleep), 2.75 *svapna* (to sleep); *vaśa* (to desire)—these, beginning with *ṣasa*, are roots with an udātta accent and are marked as having an udātta vowel for their *it* designation. And [the term] *carkarītam* [is also included].
2.76 *hnuṅ* in the sense of "removing" (*apanayana*). It is anudātta and belongs to the ātmanepada. [End of section] *vṛt*.
Thus end the adādi verbs characterized by the elision of the vikaraṇa.
3.1 *hu* "in giving and eating"; "and in taking," according to some; "also in pleasing," according to the Bhāṣya.
3.3 *hrī* in the sense of shame. Thus end the roots beginning with *ju*, which are anudātta and parasmaipada.
3.4 *pṛ* in the senses of protecting and filling;
3.5 some say *pṛ* ends in a short vowel; it is accented acute and belongs to the *parasmaipada*.
3.6 √ḍubhṛñ means "to support" and "to nourish. It is anudātta (unaccented) and is conjugated in both voices (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
3.7 *māṅ* [is used] in the senses of measuring and sound;
3.8 *ohāṅ* [is used] in the sense of going. These two are *anudātta* roots and take the *ātmanepada* endings.
3.9 *ohāk* means "to abandon. It is anudātta and belongs to the parasmaipada voice.

3.11 *ḍudhāñ* in the senses of holding and nourishing (*dhāraṇa-poṣaṇa*); some also say "giving. These two are unaccented on the root syllable (*anudātta*) and are used in both voices (*ubhayatobhāṣa*).
3.12. *ṇijir* in the sense of purification and nourishing;
3.14. *viṣḷḷi* in the sense of pervasion. Thus, the roots beginning with *ṇijir* are anudātta and have a svarita indicatory letter (*svaritet*).
Now, there are eleven roots ending in -gaṇān, belonging to the Vedic (chāndasa) tradition:
3.15 *ghṛ* in the sense of flowing and shining;
3.16 *hṛ* in the sense of acting with force.
3.18 *sṛ* (to go). *ghṛ* and the following roots are anudātta and parasmaipada.
3.19 *bhas* [is used] in the senses of threatening and shining; it is udātta and has an udātta vowel.
3.20 *ki* in the sense of knowledge; it is anudātta and belongs to the *parasmaipada*.
3.21 *kita* and 3.22 *tura* in the sense of hastening;

3.24 *dhana-dhānye* (in the sense of wealth and grain); 3.25 *jana-janane* (in the sense of producing people). Thus end the *tūr*-class roots which have an udātta vowel and are marked with an indicatory letter *ṭ*.

3.26 *gā* in the sense of praising; it is anudātta and belongs to the parasmaipada. In the Veda (*chandasi*): *vṛt*; *ghṛ* and the following eleven [roots] are used in the Veda. *iyati* is also used in the common language (*bhāṣā*). *vṛt*.
Thus end the roots such as *juhoti* and others which take the *ślu* vikaraṇa. 3.
4.1 *divu* (to play, to desire victory, to transact, to shine, to praise, to rejoice, to be intoxicated, to sleep, to love, to go). 4.2 *ṣivu* (to weave, to continue the thread).
4.3 *srivu* in the senses of moving and drying.
4.4 *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of spitting; some do not read this root.
4.5 *ṣṇusu* in the sense of eating; some say "taking" (*ādāna*), others say "disappearance" (*adarśana*).
4.7 *knasu* in the sense of bending and shining;
4.10 nṛtī (to dance or move the limbs);
4.15 *kṣip* in the sense of "to cast" or "to throw"; it is anudātta (unaccented). 4.16 *puṣp* in the sense of "to blossom.
4.20 *ṣṭīma* [are used] in the sense of becoming moist.
4.21 *vrīḍ* in the sense of inciting shame and in the sense of shame itself; 4.22 *iṣ* in the sense of motion; 4.23 *ṣah*.
4.24 *ṣuḍ* in the sense of being able;
4.25 *jṝṣ*; 4.26 *jhṝṣ* in the sense of loss of vitality. Thus end the roots of the *divādigaṇa* that are marked with an acute accent (*udātta*) on the root vowel and take the *iṭ* augment.
Now, the roots beginning with *svad* are marked as having an indicatory vowel *i* (odita).
4.28 *odūṅ* (odati) means "to burn. These two are udātta (accented) and belong to the ātmanepada voice.
4.29 *odīṅ* in the sense of destruction; 4.30 *oḍīṅ* in the sense of moving through the air;
4.32 omīṅ in the sense of injury; 4.33 orīṅ in the sense of hearing;
4.34 olīṅ in the sense of clinging.

4.35 *ovrīṅ* is used in the sense of "to choose" (*vṛṇoti*). [The root] *vṛt* [is included here]. [All roots] beginning with *svad* are marked as *odit*. 4.36 *pīṅ* is used in the sense of "drinking. 4.37 *māṅ* is used in the sense of "measuring."
4.39 *prīṅ* in the sense of affection or pleasing. These roots beginning with *dīṅ* are *ātmanebhāṣā* (middle-voiced) and have anudātta accents; however, *dīṅ* itself has an udātta accent.
4.40 *śo* in the sense of making thin; 4.41 *cho* in the sense of cutting; 4.42 *ṣo* in the sense of finishing.
4.43 *do* [is used] in the sense of cutting (*avakhaṇḍana*). Thus, the roots beginning with *śyai* are anudātta and belong to the *parasmaibhāṣā* class.
4.47 *tūrī* [is used] in the senses of moving and injuring;
